theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Resurrection of the Dead
summary: The bodily resurrection of all the dead, believers to life, unbelievers to judgment
readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 15:35-58, Daniel 12:1-3, and John 5:28-29. Today is a doctrinal pause on the resurrection of the dead. Notice the nature of the resurrection body and the two destinies.
settingTheScene: Yesterday we studied the resurrection of Christ. Today we look at his promise that his people will be raised. The Christian hope is not an immortal soul floating in a spiritual realm, though believers who die are with Christ (see Day 779). The final hope is bodily resurrection and a new creation. The Old Testament hints at it, and Jesus taught it. Paul’s answer to the question “With what kind of body do they come?” is one of the most important passages for the Christian view of the future.
observation: “And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2).
“And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above” (Daniel 12:3).
“An hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28-29).
“What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:42).
“It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44).
“Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49).
“We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet” (1 Corinthians 15:51-52).
“Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54).
doctrinalFocus:
The Bible teaches that all the dead will be raised bodily, the righteous to eternal life and the unrighteous to judgment. This is the general resurrection. Daniel 12:2 is the clearest Old Testament statement: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.” Jesus affirms it in John 5:28-29: all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, “those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.” Paul told Felix he had a hope in “a resurrection of both the just and the unjust” (Acts 24:15).

For believers, the resurrection body will be like Christ’s. Paul uses the seed analogy: there is continuity, because the same person is raised, and transformation, because the new body is much greater. It will be imperishable, glorious, powerful, and “spiritual” (that is, animated by the Spirit, not immaterial). Philippians 3:21 says Christ “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body.” We will recognize one another and be recognizable. The final state is not a disembodied existence, but a new heaven and new earth, where the redeemed live in resurrected bodies in the presence of God.

Christians have different views about the timing and sequence of the end, including whether there is a literal thousand-year reign of Christ (the millennium), whether the resurrection of the righteous and the unrighteous happen at the same time, and how Israel fits in. Premillennialists, amillennialists, and postmillennialists all affirm Christ’s personal, visible return, the bodily resurrection, the final judgment, and the new creation. The difference lies in how to read Revelation 20 and related passages. We should hold our views on timing with humility.

The practical effect of the doctrine is profound. We do not fear the grave. We treat our bodies with dignity. We care for the physical world and for the suffering. We grieve with hope. And we work with confidence, because the final word belongs to God.
interpretation:
Paul anticipates two questions: “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” He answers with an analogy: “What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel.” The seed dies and rises as a plant. God gives it a body as he has chosen. There is continuity and difference. The glories of earthly and heavenly bodies differ, as the sun, moon, and stars differ in glory.

Then the four contrasts: “What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.” Burial is sowing. The body goes into the ground like a seed. The resurrection body is not less physical than the present body, but more: it is fitted for life in the new creation, under the Spirit’s power.

Paul continues, “Thus it is written, The first man Adam became a living being; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.” Christ is the model and source of our resurrection. “Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.” Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. A change is needed.

Then the mystery: not all will die, but all will be changed “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.” The perishable body must put on the imperishable, and the mortal body immortality. When this happens, the Scripture will be fulfilled: “Death is swallowed up in victory.” Paul quotes Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 and taunts death: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But Christ has dealt with sin, and so the sting is removed.

Daniel 12:3 adds a note of glory: “Those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above, and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.” The people of God will shine. Whatever we do now in faithfulness will not be forgotten.
connection: Isaiah 25:6-9 and 26:19 anticipate the resurrection. Job 19:25-27 declares “I know that my Redeemer lives.” Ezekiel 37:1-14 is the vision of dry bones. Luke 20:27-40 records Jesus on the resurrection. John 11:21-27 records Jesus saying “I am the resurrection and the life.” Romans 8:11, 8:18-25 and 2 Corinthians 4:14 speak of future resurrection. Philippians 3:20-21 describes the transformation. 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 comforts the grieving. Revelation 20 to 22 describes the final judgment and new creation.
application:
Treat your body today as something God will raise: care for it, honor it, use it for his service.

If you have lost someone in Christ, read verses 42 to 44 and imagine them in glory.

Thank God that death is swallowed up in victory.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that he will raise the dead.
Tell him what you want to say about death in light of this.
Ask him to keep you steadfast in the meantime.
